bullet.text: Viola-Jones looked for light and dark rectangles in one frame, on one machine, where the camera happened to point. A pole reader now answers one query across 80,000 of them.
This era could tell you a face was there. It could not tell you where that face was last Tuesday. The pole networks are built to answer exactly that.
A 2000s bullet camera recorded to a tape nobody watched. Its descendant files every drive-past into an index that 4,800 cities can search.

dome.text: Landmark geometry needed a cooperative face, near, lit and roughly frontal. Smart glasses now take the same measurements from a stranger at eye level.
The dome hid which way it was pointed. The glasses hide that there is a camera at all, which is a harder problem for you and an easier one for them.
A dome was a fixed thing you could learn to avoid. A wearable moves the lens to wherever the wearer decides to stand.

cube.text: DeepFace and FaceNet turned a face into a vector. What this era lacked was reach: one house, one feed. Reach is precisely what the pole networks added.
Box cameras leaked because of default passwords. The modern leak is a police search reason, with the plate attached, indexed by Bing.
A home camera watched one doorway and told one owner. A pole reader watches a road and tells any agency the owner shares with, including the ones state law forbids.

pill.text: Depth and infrared beat the photograph and the dark. They still required you to step in front of a fixed sensor. Glasses removed the stepping in front.
This era's liveness check was state of the art and bolted to a wall. The state of the art now walks past you on someone's face.
Miniaturisation was sold as elegance. It ended the moment of notice: no housing, no blinking light, no way to tell a read happened.

street.text: Texas, 2025: a sheriff's office searched 83,345 cameras across 6,809 networks for a woman who had ended her own pregnancy, and logged it as a missing person case.
Kentucky, 2026: an officer ran 2,048 searches on his ex-girlfriend's two cars in five months, 241 of them while a protection order stood against him.
203 documented cases of plate-reader abuse since 2023: stalking exes, immigration sweeps, personal lookups. One officer searched for his ex more than 10,000 times.
Illinois police let federal agents run more than 4,000 immigration searches through a network of 40,000 cameras, in a state where that use is illegal.
In Roseville, 71% of the plate reads that triggered an alert were wrong. Elsewhere the misread of a single character put a couple at gunpoint beside their baby.
The vendor ran a webinar teaching police to watch protest crowds live, with plate readers, drones and gunshot sensors on one screen.
One volunteer mapping these cameras received a cease and desist. He refused, kept the map online, and cities began cancelling contracts.

glasses.text: Researchers analysed 350 videos of women filmed in public through smart glasses. The more covert the recording, the more severe the harassment that followed.
Two students wired a face search engine to a pair of Ray-Bans: look at a stranger, receive their name, home address, phone number and relatives.
The same two now sell always-on recording glasses at $249, with no indicator light. Their answer on consent: we trust our users to ask.
Footage from these glasses reaches human reviewers. Annotators in Nairobi described bathrooms, undressing, sex and bank cards, with the face blurring often failing.
Meta remotely disabled around 7,000 pairs whose owners had tampered with the recording light. The demand was real enough to be worth the tampering.
Homeland Security wants its own pair: face and gait recognition in the field, prototypes targeted for 2027. Agents in six states were already using consumer ones.
